symptoms: Diagnostic criteria (any one of): acute illness with skin/mucosal involvement AND respiratory compromise, hypotension, or end-organ dysfunction; OR >=2 features after exposure to a likely allergen (skin/mucosal involvement, respiratory compromise, hypotension/end-organ dysfunction, persistent GI symptoms); OR hypotension after exposure to a known allergen (SBP fall >=30%).

management_steps.details: Stop/remove the suspected allergen. Place supine and elevate legs. High-flow oxygen, monitors, IV access.
Adrenaline 1mg/ml (1:1000), 0.01mg/kg up to 0.5mg, IM into the anterolateral thigh (0.5ml adult dose).

Airway obstruction (partial): nebulised adrenaline 5mg, prepare for a difficult airway. Airway obstruction (complete): bag-mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen, prepare for a difficult airway. Wheeze/dyspnoea: continuous nebulisation with beta-2 agonists. Hypotension: crystalloid (Ringer's Lactate/Balsol) 20ml/kg, repeat as necessary — large volumes may be required.
Promethazine (Phenergan) 12.5mg slow IV (max 25mg), weight-dependent in children. Hydrocortisone (Solu-Cortef) 200mg slow IV, weight-dependent in children.

management_steps.action: Immediate Life Threat / Poor Response / Deterioration
management_steps.details: Repeat IM adrenaline every 3-5 minutes if no improvement, or start an adrenaline infusion per protocol. Cardiac arrest secondary to anaphylaxis: follow ACLS, give immediate adrenaline, consider rapid escalation to high-dose adrenaline (3-5mg every 2-3 minutes), high-volume IV fluids.

warnings: Biphasic reaction occurs in 5-20% and can recur after the initial episode. Risk factors: delayed adrenaline administration, slow response to adrenaline, need for repeated adrenaline doses, requiring IV fluids, lack of steroid use.
